widths.heading: Swing Trading
widths.mainText:
TRADING STRATEGY

Swing Trading

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. No independent professional review is claimed.

Holding positions 2-10 days to capture intermediate moves.

Practise this strategy
QUICK ANSWER
What is the Swing Trading trading strategy and does it work?

Swing Trading: Holding positions 2-10 days to capture intermediate moves. Performance depends on market regime, entry/exit rules, costs and sample size. Use the simulator to measure your own distribution of outcomes. Study context: A worksheet comparing multi-day observation windows and overnight exposure; no work schedule establishes suitability. Practise it free on TradeHQ with $100,000 in virtual cash. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Study context

A worksheet comparing multi-day observation windows and overnight exposure; no work schedule establishes suitability.

Limitations

Manual review leaves exposure between observations, and an intended exit can be crossed by a gap.

Hypothetical study steps
1
Define a multi-day observation window without implying that a holding period predicts a return.
2
Record a hypothetical entry, quantity and exit assumption before examining later observations.
3
Compare different gap sizes and exit distances, including an unfilled or worse-than-planned exit.
4
Keep fixed, partial and trailing exit rules in separate conceptual comparisons. TradeHQ does not place automatic stops.
Worked example

Hypothetical worksheet, not an observed trade: Bought NVDA at $145 after a pullback, stop $138, target $165 — risked $7 to make $20. Stop and target levels are conceptual assumptions, not resting TradeHQ orders; gaps and fees can change the result.

Where this method comes from

Swing trading describes positions held across sessions, often over days or weeks. The label does not determine a suitable position size or make the decision less consequential. A scheduled review can fit some learners’ routines, but holdings remain exposed between observations and suitability cannot be inferred from employment status. The trade-off is overnight risk — earnings, macro prints and weekend headlines all move price while your stop cannot protect you at the exact level you set.

Sample and market limitations

An apparent trend or pullback is a description of selected past data. A later continuation and a reversal are both possible. Earnings and other announcements can introduce overnight gaps; a planned exit does not guarantee a fill at that price.

Interpretation pitfalls
Treating a round-number exit or volatility multiple as guaranteed loss protection.
Assuming favorable earnings or a company narrative determines the next opening price.
Adding to a position while reporting results as though exposure had stayed fixed.
Worked arithmetic

Hypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 47% wins at 2R and 53% losses at 1R give 0.41R gross expectancy per trade. With an arbitrary $1,000 practice loss amount, that is $410 before costs. These assumed inputs do not establish performance. Losing-run probabilities require a sample length and independence assumption; no particular run is guaranteed or universally normal.

Figures are illustrative teaching examples, not projections of your results. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Realistic expectations

Performance depends on market regime, entry/exit rules, costs and sample size. Use the simulator to measure your own distribution of outcomes.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Where this method comes from

Swing trading describes positions held across sessions, often over days or weeks. The label does not determine a suitable position size or make the decision less consequential. A scheduled review can fit some learners’ routines, but holdings remain exposed between observations and suitability cannot be inferred from employment status. The trade-off is overnight risk — earnings, macro prints and weekend headlines all move price while your stop cannot protect you at the exact level you set.

Sample and market limitations

An apparent trend or pullback is a description of selected past data. A later continuation and a reversal are both possible. Earnings and other announcements can introduce overnight gaps; a planned exit does not guarantee a fill at that price.

Interpretation pitfalls
Treating a round-number exit or volatility multiple as guaranteed loss protection.
Assuming favorable earnings or a company narrative determines the next opening price.
Adding to a position while reporting results as though exposure had stayed fixed.
